Axial Skeleton
• The part of skeleton that consist of the bones of the Head and Trunk
• Consist of 80 bones
• Consist of six parts : 
a) Skull
b) The Ossicle of middle ear
c) The Hyoid Bones
d) The rib
e) Sternum
f)
Vertebrae


--- Slide/Halaman 5 ---
Skull
• A bony structure that supports the face and forms a protective 
cavity for the brain
• Formed by intramembranous ossification
• Joined together by sutures (fibrous joints
• The skull can be divided into two groups:
a) Neurocranium : Calvarium and Basis Cranii
b) Viscerocranium


--- Slide/Halaman 6 ---
Human Skull – 22 bones
1. Neurocranium (8 bones fused at sutures) – protects brain, 
provides muscle attachment, sinuses reduce weight of skull
• Calvarium : Os Frontale, Os Parietale and Os Occipitale
• Basis Cranii : Os Frontale, Os sphenoidale, Os ethmoidale, Os
Occipitale, Os Parietale and Os temporale
2. Viscerocranium (Facial bones) (14 bones) – gives shape to face, 
provides muscle attachment


--- Slide/Halaman 7 ---
Neurocranium


--- Slide/Halaman 8 ---
Sutures of the skull
• Sutures are of clinical importance, as they can be points of potential 
weakness in both childhood and adulthood. The main sutures in 
adulthood are:
1. Sutura Coronalis which fuses the frontal bone with the two 
parietal bones.
2. Sutura Sagitalis which fuses both parietal bones to each other.
3. Sutura Lambdoidea which fuses the occipital bone to the two 
parietal bones.

Backbones/Collumna Vertebrae


--- Slide/Halaman 21 ---
Vertebral Column/Columna Vertebrae
• The vertebral column is a vertical series of approximately 33 small 
bones
• Known as vertebrae
• Separated by intervertebral discs/discus intervertebralis
• Separated into five different regions
• Different region characterised by a different vertebral structure.
• Each vertebrae is given a name according to its location


--- Slide/Halaman 22 ---
What is the functions?
The vertebral column has four main functions:
• Protection – encloses and protects the spinal cord within the spinal 
canal.
• Support – carries the weight of the body above the pelvis.
• Axis – forms the central axis of the body.
• Movement – has roles in both posture and movement.

• Vertebrae coccygeal: 3~4 (à coccyx)

General structure of vertebrae
• Corpus vertebrae located anterior
• Arcus vertebrae located posterior
• Pediculus: 
• Incisura vertebrae sup. dan inf. à foramen 
intervertebralis
• Lamina consists of: 
• processus (7): 
• process spinousus (1)
• process transversus (2)
• processus articularis sup. dan inf. (4)
• foramen vertebralis àVertebral canal

Regional variations of vertebrae
Vertebrae cervicalis
• Corpus vertebrae: small
• foramen vertebralis: larger; triangular
• processes spinosus: 
• C3-C5: short & bifida
• C6: long
• C7: longest; not bifida
• processus transversus: short, bifida, foramen 
transversum
• processus articular: horizontal

Clinical correlation:
• Scoliosis; kyphosis; lordosis
• Laminectomy
• Surgical removal of the processus spinosus and their supporting 
lamina vertebralis à to relieve pressure on the corda spinalis or nerve 
root caused by blood clot, tumor, herniated/ruptured discus 
intervertebralis
• Coccygeal trauma; fx-dislocation of the sacrococcygeal joint
Note: 
In aging, decrease of height (0,5- 2cm) occur between the ages 50-55 because
of
compression
and
shrinkage
of
the
discus
intervertebralis
which
collectively account for 25% of the height of columna vertebralis.

Sternum
• The sternum is a flat bone located at the anterior aspect of the 
thorax. 
• The sternum helps protect the internal thoracic viscera – such as the 
heart, lungs and oesophagus
• The sternum can be divided into three parts; 
1. Manubrium Sterni
2. Corpus Sterni
3. Processus Xiphoideus
